statement: The supplied sources genuinely contain nothing to derive, as a Lie algebra is an algebraic definition and object rather than a derived result (the heading 'Derivations' in the source refers to algebraic derivations D: A -> A satisfying the Leibniz rule, not a mathematical derivation or proof). A Lie algebra g over a field F is a vector space equipped with a bilinear Lie bracket [·, ·] satisfying the Jacobi identity and vanishing on identical elements ([X, X] = 0). For a matrix Lie group G ⊂ GL(n, R), the corresponding Lie algebra is defined as the tangent space at the identity matrix I: g = {X = c'(0) ∈ M_n(R) : smooth c: R -> G, c(0) = I}, equipped with the commutator Lie bracket [X, Y] = XY - YX.

symbols.meaning: Lie algebra (a vector space over field F or tangent space to G at identity)
Lie bracket operation (bilinear map g x g -> g)
Matrix Lie group of invertible matrices in GL(n, R)
Space of real n x n matrices
Smooth curve in Lie group G passing through identity at t = 0
Elements (tangent vectors or matrices) in the Lie algebra g
Adjoint mapping / inner derivation defined by ad_x(y) = [x, y]
Space of derivations of an algebra A over field F

properties.why: For a matrix Lie algebra g ⊂ gl(n, R), the Lie bracket of tangent vectors at the identity is given by the matrix commutator [X, Y] = XY - YX
The axioms of a Lie algebra imply that [X, X] = 0 for any element X

properties.property: Adjoint mapping is an inner derivation
properties.why: The adjoint mapping ad_x(y) := [x, y] satisfies the derivation Leibniz rule ad_x([y, z]) = [ad_x(y), z] + [y, ad_x(z)] as a consequence of the Jacobi identity

properties.property: Derivations of an algebra form a Lie algebra
properties.why: The commutator of two derivations [D_1, D_2] := D_1 D_2 - D_2 D_1 is again a derivation, making Der_F(A) into a Lie algebra
Every one-dimensional linear subspace of a Lie algebra g is closed under bracket with [X, X] = 0, though it need not be an ideal
For two Lie algebras g and g', the direct product g x g' with bracket [(x, x'), (y, y')] = ([x, y], [x', y']) forms a Lie algebra whose direct summands commute: [(x, 0), (0, x')] = 0

properties.property: Semidirect product from a split extension
properties.why: If g has an ideal i and the canonical projection g -> g/i admits a section as a Lie algebra homomorphism, g splits as g = g/i ⋉ i

assumptions.assumption: Linear vector space and underlying field structure
assumptions.breaks_when: The underlying set does not admit a vector space structure over a field F or scalar operations fail

assumptions.assumption: Smoothness of curves in matrix groups at identity
assumptions.breaks_when: Curves c: R -> G are not differentiable at t = 0, or G is not a Lie group

failure_modes.signature: Bracket [A, B] of elements in a linear subspace produces an element outside the subspace
failure_modes.cause: The subspace is merely a linear subspace and not closed under the commutator bracket, failing to be a Lie subalgebra

failure_modes.mode: Subalgebra fails to be an ideal
failure_modes.signature: Bracket [X, Y] with X in the subalgebra and Y in g does not lie in the subalgebra
failure_modes.cause: A subalgebra (such as a 1-dimensional abelian subalgebra) is closed under internal brackets but does not absorb brackets with general elements of g
The Lie algebra g is not semisimple over characteristic zero (e.g., an abelian Lie algebra V where Out_F(V) is isomorphic to gl(V))
